editor_spans.body: Last week I called the Prime Minister's offer to Holyrood mostly a way of putting the Scottish Government on the spot, because Westminster cannot create Scottish regional bodies itself. The full speech adds something the 15 October trailer left out, and I need to correct that reading. He has offered 'DWP devolution', meaning a localised employment support model 'shaped by Holyrood'. Unlike regional structures, this is a power Westminster actually holds and can give away. It makes the offer more than a political trap. The price is in the conditions: the scheme must 'go deep', 'right down', and be built on 'the Easterhouse principle'. Otherwise, in his words, 'it won't work'. So Edinburgh would get the power only if it agrees to pass it down again. No previous devolution deal has asked Holyrood for that.

Look at how the speech tells its history. Ravenscraig closed by 'a decision taken hundreds of miles away'. Leigh's pits shut and 'No one in Whitehall' planned what came next. That is the argument Scottish nationalism has made against London for forty years. Here a UK Prime Minister makes it himself, then turns it so the dividing line runs between any distant centre and its places, not between Scotland and England. Holyrood counts as one of those centres: Scotland is 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe', and 'UK level, Holyrood level' have both let places down. Easterhouse is offered back to Scotland as a Scottish idea that was ignored at home. The argument is aimed at the SNP's own ground. It does not attack independence. It goes after the SNP's record of keeping power in Edinburgh.

The first real test is close and has a date. The National Economic Council will meet the leaders of the devolved governments 'in a couple of weeks', the first such meeting since he took office. The speech also skips the hardest Scottish economic issue. Aberdeen gets one sentence and a promise of 'more to say in due course'. 'The next generation of energy jobs' gets no detail. Grangemouth and the North Sea are where a plan to reindustrialise Scotland will succeed or fail, so it matters more what he eventually says about Aberdeen than how many regional bodies get created.

S353 (mentioning Andy Burnham {Q269909}, Scotland’s First Minister {E420}, Parliament of the United Kingdom {Q11010}, Scottish Parliament {Q206171}): In a speech today, the Prime Minister will invite Scotland’s First Minister to work with ⟦Andy Burnham⟧ on the common good of pushing more power out of both Westminster and Holyrood, unlocking jobs and opportunity in every region.
